title: Pharmacology
tagline: How drugs act, how the body handles drugs, adverse effects and safe prescribing
summary: Every treatment depends on understanding how drugs act and how the body handles them. This course covers drug targets and dose–response relationships, absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, the arithmetic of dosing and drug monitoring, drugs acting on the autonomic nervous system, adverse reactions and interactions, differences between patients, and how medicines are developed, regulated and prescribed safely.
overview: Pharmacology explains why a medicine works, why it sometimes harms, and why the same dose can suit one person and endanger another. Two questions run through the course: what the drug does to the body (pharmacodynamics) and what the body does to the drug (pharmacokinetics). Answering them turns prescribing from memorising doses into reasoning from a small number of principles.

The course begins with drug targets, the law of mass action, agonists and antagonists, potency and efficacy, and the dose–response curves that underlie the therapeutic index. It then follows a dose through the body: crossing membranes, routes of administration and bioavailability, volume of distribution and protein binding, metabolism by cytochrome P450 and conjugating enzymes, renal and biliary excretion, clearance and half-life. These quantities are combined into loading and maintenance doses, the four-to-five half-life rule for steady state, therapeutic drug monitoring and dose adjustment in kidney disease, with worked calculations throughout.

The autonomic nervous system serves as a map for a large group of everyday drugs, from β-blockers and salbutamol to atropine, adrenaline and neuromuscular blockers. Later chapters cover adverse drug reactions, drug allergy and interactions; variation between patients through age, body size, organ function, pregnancy and genetics; and the path from drug discovery through clinical trials, licensing and cost-effectiveness appraisal to rational, safe prescribing and stewardship. Doses appear only as illustrative values; real prescribing follows a current formulary and local guidance.
outcomes: Explain how drugs act on receptors, ion channels, enzymes and transporters, and use occupancy, efficacy, potency and the dose ratio to interpret dose–response curves and antagonism.
Describe how drugs cross membranes and are absorbed by different routes, and calculate and interpret bioavailability, volume of distribution and the effects of ionisation and protein binding.
Explain phase I and phase II metabolism and renal and biliary excretion, and predict the consequences of enzyme induction and inhibition.
Calculate clearance, half-life, loading and maintenance doses and time to steady state, and recognise saturable (zero-order) elimination.
Interpret drug levels in therapeutic drug monitoring, including sample timing, steady state and protein binding, and adjust doses for kidney function.
Use the transmitters and receptors of the autonomic nervous system to predict the effects, uses and adverse effects of cholinergic, antimuscarinic, neuromuscular blocking and adrenergic drugs.
Classify adverse drug reactions, recognise severe hypersensitivity syndromes and important interactions, assess causality and explain pharmacovigilance and Yellow Card reporting.
Account for differences between patients due to age, body size, organ function, pregnancy, breastfeeding, genetic variation and adherence when choosing a medicine and dose.

Outline drug development from target to post-marketing surveillance, interpret trial results and cost-effectiveness, and apply the principles of rational prescribing, prescription safety and stewardship.

history.title: An active principle isolated
history.detail: Friedrich Sertürner, a German pharmacist's assistant, begins isolating morphine from opium, the first alkaloid obtained from a plant drug. Studying a pure substance instead of a crude preparation made it possible to relate dose to effect.

history.title: A receptive substance
history.detail: John Newport Langley, studying nicotine and curare on skeletal muscle, proposes a 'receptive substance' on muscle cells with which drugs combine. With Paul Ehrlich's side-chain theory, this becomes the receptor concept.

history.title: Chemical transmission
history.detail: Otto Loewi shows that stimulating the vagus nerve of a frog heart releases a substance that slows a second heart; it is later identified as acetylcholine. Loewi and Henry Dale share the 1936 Nobel Prize.

history.title: The sulfanilamide elixir
history.detail: More than a hundred people in the United States die after taking sulfanilamide dissolved in diethylene glycol. The 1938 Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act requires evidence of safety before a medicine is marketed.

history.title: Alpha and beta receptors
history.detail: Raymond Ahlquist proposes two types of adrenoceptor, α and β, from the order of potency of catecholamines on different tissues. The same year, the Medical Research Council's randomised trial of streptomycin, designed with Austin Bradford Hill, sets the standard for testing treatments.

history.title: Pharmacogenetics proposed
history.detail: Arno Motulsky argues that inherited differences in enzymes explain some unexpected drug reactions, after the discovery of G6PD deficiency and plasma cholinesterase variants. Friedrich Vogel names the field pharmacogenetics in 1959.

history.title: Thalidomide
history.detail: William McBride and Widukind Lenz link thalidomide to severe limb malformations, and the drug is withdrawn. The disaster leads to the US Kefauver–Harris amendments of 1962 and, in the UK, to the Committee on Safety of Drugs and its Yellow Card scheme in 1964.

history.title: Designing a β-blocker
history.detail: James Black's propranolol, designed from Ahlquist's receptor theory, enters clinical use in the mid-1960s; Black later designs the H₂ antagonist cimetidine and shares the 1988 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

history.title: Dosing by kidney function
history.detail: Donald Cockcroft and Henry Gault publish an equation for estimating creatinine clearance from serum creatinine, age and weight; it remains part of drug licensing and dose adjustment.

history.title: TGN1412
history.detail: Six healthy volunteers in London develop life-threatening cytokine release after the first human doses of an immunostimulatory antibody. The review that follows changes how first-in-human doses of high-risk medicines are chosen, using the minimal anticipated biological effect level.

references.title: Rang and Dale's Pharmacology (9th edition)
references.authors: Ritter JM, Flower RJ, Henderson G, Loke YK, MacEwan D, Rang HP
references.note: Standard UK textbook of pharmacology, covering receptor theory, pharmacokinetics and drugs by system.

references.title: Clinical Pharmacology (11th edition)
references.authors: Bennett PN, Brown MJ, Sharma P
references.note: Clinically oriented text on prescribing, pharmacokinetics, adverse reactions and therapeutics.

references.title: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics (14th edition)
references.note: Comprehensive reference on drug mechanisms, pharmacokinetics and therapeutic use.

references.title: Clinical Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics: Concepts and Applications (4th edition)
references.note: The standard account of clearance, volume, half-life, dosing regimens and drug monitoring.

references.title: British National Formulary (BNF)
references.note: UK reference for indications, doses, cautions, interactions and monitoring; continuously updated online.

references.authors: de Vries TPGM, Henning RH, Hogerzeil HV, Fresle DA (World Health Organization)
references.note: The WHO six-step approach to rational prescribing used in this course.
